questions.stem: A non-current asset is first recorded at:
options: the value the owner believes it will have in future
its purchase price including the GST paid on it
its cost, including the costs of getting it ready for use
its expected selling price at the very end of its useful life
questions.explanation: A non-current asset is recorded at cost: the purchase price plus costs such as delivery and installation needed to get it ready for use. GST is excluded because the business claims it back as a GST credit.

questions.stem: A bakery buys a new oven. The list price is $12,000, delivery costs $300, installation costs $700 and a 12-month service contract costs $500 (all excluding GST). At what cost is the oven recorded?
questions.explanation: Cost includes the price plus the delivery and installation needed to get the oven working: 12,000 + 300 + 700 = $13,000. The service contract covers the year of use, so it is an expense; including it gives $13,500.

questions.stem: Which of these costs is included in the cost of a new delivery van?
options: Fuel for the van's first full week of deliveries
The van's first annual comprehensive insurance premium
A routine service once the van has done 10,000 km
Fitting shelving in the van before it is first used
questions.explanation: Shelving fitted before use is part of getting the van ready for its intended purpose, so it is added to cost. Fuel, annual insurance and routine servicing are running costs of using the van, so they are expenses.

questions.stem: Lakeside Joinery buys a second-hand saw for $6,000. Before it can be used, it needs $800 of repairs and $200 to transport it to the workshop (all excluding GST). At what cost is the saw recorded?
questions.explanation: Repairs needed before first use and the transport to the workshop are both costs of getting the saw ready for use, so cost = 6,000 + 800 + 200 = $7,000. Repairs made later, once the saw is in use, would be an expense instead.

questions.stem: In the Balance Sheet, what does the carrying value of a non-current asset represent?
options: its cost less its residual value
its depreciation for the current year
its cost less accumulated depreciation
its expected selling price today
questions.explanation: Carrying value is the cost of the asset less all the depreciation recorded on it so far, as shown in the Balance Sheet. Cost less residual value is the depreciable amount spread over the asset's life.

questions.stem: Residual value is:
options: the total depreciation charged over the asset's whole life
the expected value of the asset when its useful life ends
the asset's cost less its accumulated depreciation to date
the price the asset would sell for at today's market prices
questions.explanation: Residual value is an estimate of what the asset will be worth when the business stops using it. Cost less accumulated depreciation is carrying value, which is a different measure.

questions.stem: Why can the carrying value of a non-current asset differ from what it could be sold for?
options: A non-current asset cannot be recorded until it has been paid for in full
Useful life and residual value are estimates, and depreciation is not a valuation
The original cost of the asset is never shown on the supplier's tax invoice for it
Depreciation must be set equal to the fall in the asset's market value each year
questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads the asset's cost over its estimated useful life; it does not track market value. Because life and residual value are estimates, the carrying value seldom equals the selling price.

questions.stem: Useful life is:
options: the period over which the business repays the loan for the asset
the period for which the supplier's warranty covers the asset
the period over which the business expects to use the asset
the number of years until the asset has a carrying value of zero
questions.explanation: Useful life is the business's estimate of how long it will use the asset, and depreciation is spread over this period. It is not tied to the loan term or the warranty, and an asset with a residual value never reaches zero.

questions.stem: In the Income Statement, depreciation of a non-current asset is reported as:
options: an expense that reduces net profit
a revenue that increases net profit
a deduction from the asset's cost
a cash payment in operating activities
questions.explanation: Depreciation is the part of the asset's cost used up in the period, so it is an expense. Deducting Accumulated Depreciation from cost happens in the Balance Sheet, not the Income Statement.

questions.stem: A café buys a coffee machine for $26,000 with a residual value of $2,000 and a useful life of 4 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life = (26,000 − 2,000) ÷ 4 = $6,000. Ignoring the residual value gives $6,500, and $24,000 is the total depreciation over the 4 years.

questions.stem: Shop furniture costs $15,000, has a residual value of $3,000 and a useful life of 6 years. Using straight-line depreciation, what is its carrying value after 3 full years?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = (15,000 − 3,000) ÷ 6 = $2,000, so accumulated depreciation after 3 years is $6,000 and the carrying value is 15,000 − 6,000 = $9,000. $6,000 is the accumulated depreciation, not the carrying value.

questions.stem: A machine is bought on 1 October for $40,000 with a residual value of $4,000 and a useful life of 5 years. The business's year ends on 30 June. What is the straight-line depreciation for the first year?
questions.explanation: A full year's depreciation is (40,000 − 4,000) ÷ 5 = $7,200, but the machine was used for only 9 months, so depreciation = 7,200 × 9/12 = $5,400. Charging a full year gives $7,200, and ignoring the residual value gives $6,000.

questions.stem: Under the straight-line method, the depreciation expense is:
options: a fixed percentage of the carrying value each year
equal to the change in the asset's market value
the same amount in every full year of the asset's life
highest in the first year and lower in each later year
questions.explanation: Straight-line spreads the depreciable amount evenly, so each full year has the same charge. A falling charge and a percentage of carrying value describe the reducing balance method.

questions.stem: Equipment costs $50,000 and has a residual value of $5,000. The straight-line depreciation is $9,000 a year. What useful life has been estimated?
options: 5.6 years
6.1 years
4.5 years
5 years
questions.explanation: Useful life = (cost − residual value) ÷ annual depreciation = 45,000 ÷ 9,000 = 5 years. Dividing the full $50,000 cost gives about 5.6 years, which ignores the residual value.

questions.stem: Under the reducing balance method, depreciation for each year is calculated as:
options: the difference between the asset's cost and market value
a fixed percentage of the carrying value at the start of each year
a fixed percentage of the asset's original cost in every year
(cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, the same each year
questions.explanation: Reducing balance applies the same rate to a carrying value that falls each year, so the charge falls too. Applying the rate to the original cost would give the same charge every year, like straight-line.

questions.stem: A delivery vehicle costs $48,000 and is depreciated at 25% a year using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation in the second year?
questions.explanation: Year 1 depreciation is 25% × $48,000 = $12,000, leaving a carrying value of $36,000. Year 2 depreciation is 25% × $36,000 = $9,000. Applying the rate to cost again gives $12,000, and $21,000 is the accumulated depreciation after two years.

questions.stem: Equipment costing $10,000 is depreciated at 40% a year using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation in the third year?
questions.explanation: Year 1: 40% × 10,000 = 4,000, leaving 6,000. Year 2: 40% × 6,000 = 2,400, leaving 3,600. Year 3: 40% × 3,600 = $1,440. $2,160 is the carrying value left after year 3, not the depreciation.

questions.stem: Which statement about the reducing balance method is correct?
options: Depreciation is the same amount in every year of the asset's life
The method ignores the asset's carrying value in its calculation
The asset is depreciated to a carrying value of exactly zero
Depreciation is highest in year 1 and falls in each later year
questions.explanation: Because the rate is applied to a falling carrying value, depreciation is largest in year 1 and smaller each year. A percentage of a positive amount never reaches zero, so the asset is not depreciated to nil.

questions.stem: Which asset is best suited to the reducing balance method?
options: A computer giving most of its benefit in its first years
Shop fittings that give equal benefit over ten years
Office furniture that is used evenly in each year of its life
A display cabinet that is used the same amount every year
questions.explanation: Reducing balance charges more depreciation early, which matches an asset that gives more of its benefit, or loses value fastest, in its early years. Assets used evenly over their lives suit straight-line.

questions.stem: An asset costs $30,000, has a residual value of $6,000 and a useful life of 4 years. The reducing balance rate is 30%. Compared with straight-line, choosing reducing balance in the first year gives:
options: depreciation $3,000 higher, so the carrying value is $3,000 higher at year end
depreciation $3,000 higher, so net profit and carrying value are $3,000 lower
depreciation $3,000 higher, so cash at bank is $3,000 lower than otherwise
depreciation $3,000 lower, so net profit and carrying value are $3,000 higher
questions.explanation: Straight-line gives (30,000 − 6,000) ÷ 4 = $6,000, and reducing balance gives 30% × 30,000 = $9,000, so depreciation is $3,000 higher. This lowers net profit and the carrying value by $3,000. Depreciation involves no cash, so the bank balance is the same under either method.

questions.stem: Choosing the depreciation method that matches the pattern in which an asset's benefits are used up supports which qualitative characteristic?
options: Understandability
Faithful representation
Timeliness
Verifiability
questions.explanation: Matching the method to how the asset is actually used gives an expense and carrying value that reflect the real economic event. Timeliness and verifiability are about when information is available and whether it can be checked.

questions.stem: Once a business has chosen a depreciation method for an asset, why should it apply that method consistently?
options: So its reports can be compared from one period to the next
Because changing methods changes the cash paid for the asset
Because the period assumption forbids any change of method
So the asset's carrying value always equals its market value
questions.explanation: Changing methods each year would mean differences in profit came from the method, not from performance, which destroys comparability. The cash paid for the asset was fixed at purchase, whichever method is used.

questions.stem: Which General Journal entry records depreciation for the year?
options: Debit Depreciation, credit Accumulated Depreciation
Debit Accumulated Depreciation, credit Depreciation
Debit Depreciation, credit Bank
Debit the asset account, credit Depreciation
questions.explanation: Depreciation is an expense, so it is debited, and Accumulated Depreciation is credited to build up the total written off the asset. No cash is involved, so Bank is not affected.

questions.stem: Which source document authorises the recording of depreciation for the year?
options: A statement of account
A memo
A purchase invoice
A bank statement
questions.explanation: Depreciation is an internal transaction with no outside party, so it is supported by a memo. A purchase invoice is the evidence for the original purchase of the asset.

questions.stem: In the Balance Sheet, Accumulated Depreciation is reported as:
options: an expense for the year
a deduction from the asset's cost
a non-current liability
a current liability
questions.explanation: Accumulated Depreciation is a negative asset: it is subtracted from the asset's cost to show the carrying value. It is not owed to anyone, so it is not a liability.

questions.stem: Depreciation is reported as an expense in the Income Statement. How does it appear in the Cash Flow Statement?
options: As an operating outflow equal to the depreciation expense
As an investing outflow equal to the depreciation expense
As a financing outflow equal to the depreciation expense
It does not appear, because depreciation involves no cash
questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset already paid for, so no cash moves when it is recorded. The cash outflow was reported when the asset was bought, as an investing activity.

questions.stem: A vehicle cost $36,000. Accumulated depreciation was $12,000 at the start of the year, and depreciation for the year is $6,000. How is the vehicle reported in the Balance Sheet at the end of the year?
options: Vehicle $36,000 less Accumulated Depreciation $18,000, carrying value $18,000
Vehicle $36,000 less Accumulated Depreciation $6,000, carrying value $30,000
Vehicle $36,000 less Accumulated Depreciation $12,000, carrying value $24,000
Vehicle $30,000 less Accumulated Depreciation $12,000, carrying value $18,000
questions.explanation: Accumulated depreciation is the total so far: 12,000 + 6,000 = $18,000, so the carrying value is 36,000 − 18,000 = $18,000. The Balance Sheet shows the asset at its original cost with the full accumulated depreciation deducted.

questions.stem: A business buys equipment for cash and records depreciation of $2,000 on it in the first year. Which statement is correct?
options: The purchase is an investing outflow; depreciation reduces profit only
The purchase is an expense; depreciation is an investing outflow
Both the purchase and the depreciation are operating outflows
The purchase reduces profit; the depreciation reduces cash
questions.explanation: Buying equipment is an investing cash outflow, but it is not an expense because the equipment is an asset. Depreciation then gradually expenses the cost, reducing profit without any cash moving.

questions.stem: A shop records depreciation of $4,000 on its fittings for the year. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
options: Liabilities increase by $4,000 and owner's equity decreases by $4,000
Assets decrease by $4,000 and liabilities decrease by $4,000
Assets increase by $4,000 and owner's equity decreases by $4,000
Assets decrease by $4,000 and owner's equity decreases by $4,000
questions.explanation: Accumulated Depreciation reduces the carrying value of the fittings, so assets fall, and the depreciation expense reduces owner's equity. Treating Accumulated Depreciation as a liability is a common error.

questions.stem: A business's total assets were $160,000 at the start of the year and $200,000 at the end. Its net profit was $27,000. What is its return on assets?
questions.explanation: Average total assets = (160,000 + 200,000) ÷ 2 = $180,000, and return on assets = 27,000 ÷ 180,000 × 100 = 15%. Using only the closing assets gives 13.5%, and not halving the total gives 7.5%.

questions.stem: A business buys a $50,000 machine with a bank loan, but its net sales do not change during the year. What happens to its asset turnover?
options: It falls, as average total assets rise with no extra sales
It rises, as the business now has more productive assets
It is unchanged, as the loan offsets the cost of the machine
It falls, because buying the machine reduces net sales
questions.explanation: Asset turnover = net sales ÷ average total assets, so higher assets with the same sales means a lower figure. The loan is a liability and does not offset assets in this indicator.

questions.stem: Which non-financial information would best help an owner decide whether to replace a machine?
options: The machine's carrying value in the latest Balance Sheet
The business's return on assets for the latest year
The number of breakdowns and hours of downtime each month
The depreciation expense charged on the machine this year
questions.explanation: Breakdowns and downtime measure how well the machine is working and are counted in events and hours, not dollars. Depreciation, carrying value and return on assets are all financial figures.

questions.stem: Other things being equal, which action would increase a business's return on assets?
options: Increasing the depreciation rate on equipment
Paying higher wages for the same output
Selling unused equipment at its carrying value
Buying extra equipment that then sits idle
questions.explanation: Selling idle equipment at its carrying value lowers average total assets without changing profit, so return on assets rises. Idle new equipment raises assets without raising profit, and higher expenses reduce profit.

questions.stem: An asset register is:
options: a record of each non-current asset's cost, location and depreciation
a list of the amounts still owed to suppliers for non-current assets
a special journal for recording cash purchases of non-current assets
the section of the Balance Sheet that lists non-current assets
questions.explanation: An asset register keeps details of each asset, such as its cost, supplier, location, serial number, depreciation and servicing. Amounts owed to suppliers are recorded in Accounts Payable.

questions.stem: How does an asset register help to safeguard non-current assets?
options: It records each asset's cash payment in the Cash Flow Statement
It allows physical checks that each recorded asset still exists
It removes the need to depreciate each of the business's assets
It allows the business to claim GST on second-hand assets
questions.explanation: Because the register lists each asset and where it should be, the business can check the assets are still there and detect theft or loss. Assets are still depreciated whether or not a register is kept.

questions.stem: Regular servicing of a business's equipment mainly helps to:
options: remove the need to record depreciation on the equipment
turn the equipment into a current asset of the business
allow the equipment to be recorded at its market value
extend the equipment's useful life and reduce breakdowns
questions.explanation: Maintenance keeps equipment working and lasting longer, which reduces downtime and delays the cost of replacement. It does not change how the asset is classified or valued in the reports.

questions.stem: A florist is deciding whether to buy a $30,000 van with a bank loan or lease one for $8,000 a year. Which consideration favours leasing?
options: Owning the van so that it can be sold at the end of its useful life
Avoiding all interest, maintenance and running costs of a van
Being able to depreciate the van using the reducing balance method
Avoiding a large initial outlay, preserving the business's cash
questions.explanation: Leasing spreads the cost over regular payments, so the business keeps cash for other needs. Owning and later selling the van are advantages of buying, and a leased van still needs fuel and other running costs.

questions.stem: Non-current assets are reported at cost less accumulated depreciation, not at what they would sell for if the business closed. Which assumption allows this?
options: Period
Accrual basis
Going concern
Accounting entity
questions.explanation: Because the business is assumed to continue operating, its assets will be used rather than sold off, so a closing-down sale value is not relevant. The entity assumption is about separating the owner's affairs from the business's.

questions.stem: To show a higher profit to a possible buyer, an owner extends the estimated useful life of equipment from 4 years to 10 years without any reason. What is the effect?
options: Depreciation is understated, so cash at bank is overstated
Depreciation is understated, so net profit and assets are overstated
Depreciation is overstated, so net profit and assets are understated
Cash at bank is overstated and liabilities are understated
questions.explanation: A longer life spreads the cost over more years, so each year's depreciation falls and both profit and carrying value rise. This misleads the buyer and breaches faithful representation. Depreciation involves no cash, so the bank balance is unaffected.

questions.stem: A business chooses energy-efficient refrigeration that costs more than standard equipment. What is the likely effect on its reports?
options: Higher revenue, recorded as soon as the equipment is bought
Lower electricity costs, recorded as a non-current asset
Higher depreciation each year, partly offset by lower power costs
Lower depreciation, because the equipment is energy-efficient
questions.explanation: A higher cost means more to depreciate, raising the depreciation expense, while lower electricity use reduces another expense. The owner weighs the overall effect on profit against the environmental benefit.
